summary: Specifies the syntax and processing of an Evidence Record, a structure for supporting long-term proof that data existed and was unchanged, including signed data, over a long and uncertain period. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A stamped receipt that can still prove a document existed and has not changed, even many years later.

questions: how to prove data existed long term
subtitle: A format for renewable timestamp proofs that show data existed and was unchanged, even decades later.

tldr.problem: Digitally signed data may need to be archived for 30 years or more, but hash and public key algorithms can weaken and certificates can become invalid, which makes old signatures less trustworthy.
tldr.mechanism: An Evidence Record holds Archive Timestamps, each a timestamp over the root of a Merkle hash tree of data objects. Before an algorithm weakens, the record is renewed with a new Archive Timestamp that covers the old one.
tldr.outcome: Anyone can later check that data existed at a given time, provided the last Archive Timestamp is still valid. It is a Proposed Standard and the RFC does not define a protocol for talking to an archive service.

today: RFC 4998 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2007. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Long-Term Evidence Is Needed
sections.content:
Digital signatures show data integrity and source authentication, but their reliability over long periods is not absolute. During an archival period of 30 years or more, hash algorithms and public key algorithms can become weak or certificates can become invalid, which increases the likelihood that forgeries can be created.

To keep the security of signed data, you must prove that it existed before such an event. A timestamp can do that, but some timestamps rely on mechanisms that suffer the same problems. The answer is to renew timestamps by obtaining a new one that covers the original data and its timestamps before the old mechanisms are compromised. Evidence Record Syntax (ERS) is the format that supports this renewal.

ERS generalizes the optional Archive Timestamp attribute from RFC 3126 to data of any format and takes the long-term archive requirements of RFC 4810 into account, in particular large sets of data objects. It does not define a protocol for interacting with a long-term archive system.
sections.eli5: Locks can get weaker as thieves invent new tricks. So before the lock gets old, you put a new, stronger lock over the old one.

sections.title: The Evidence Record and Its Parts
sections.content:
An Evidence Record proves the existence of an archived data object, or a group of objects such as a document and its signature, at a certain time. It can be stored separately as a file or integrated into the data, for example as an attribute.

The record is an ASN.1 SEQUENCE with these fields:

  • version: set to 1; an implementation SHOULD reject lower values.
  • digestAlgorithms: all hash algorithms used over the archival period.
  • cryptoInfos (optional): validation data such as trust anchors, certificates, revocation information or algorithm suitability. It is not protected by any timestamp, so it should be verifiable by other means.
  • encryptionInfo (optional): data needed to handle encrypted content.
  • archiveTimeStampSequence: the chains of Archive Timestamps.

To generate a record, you select the data, create the initial Archive Timestamp, and renew it when necessary. To verify, you select the data, re-encrypt it if needed, and verify the Archive Timestamp Sequence.
sections.eli5: The record is a folder. It holds the stamps, a note about which tools made them, and any extra papers needed to check them later.

sections.title: Archive Timestamps and Hash Trees
sections.content:
An Archive Timestamp is a timestamp plus lists of hash values. The lists come from reducing an ordered Merkle hash tree whose leaves are the hashes of the data objects. Each inner node is the hash of its concatenated children, and only the root hash is timestamped. Deleting one object does not affect the provability of the others.

The ArchiveTimeStamp has an optional digestAlgorithm (if absent, the timestamp's own digest algorithm is used), optional attributes, an optional reducedHashtree and the timeStamp itself, for example an RFC 3161 token. Without a reduced hash tree it is just an ordinary timestamp over one object.

To build the tree, hash each object, sort the hashes in binary ascending order within each group, concatenate and hash them, and repeat until one root remains. To prove one object, keep only the sibling hashes at each level up to the root. The parent nodes are not stored because they can be computed.

To verify, hash the data object, find the hash in the first list, hash each list upward, and finally check that the root matches the hashed message in the timestamp. The data needed to verify the timestamp, such as certificates, MUST be preserved.
sections.eli5: Imagine fingerprints of many papers combined pair by pair into one master fingerprint, and only that master gets stamped. To prove one paper, you only show the few fingerprints along its path up.

sections.title: Renewal: Chains and Sequences
sections.content:
An Archive Timestamp can become invalid if the hash or public key algorithm in it weakens, or if the timestamp authority certificate expires or is revoked. Two kinds of renewal exist.

  • Timestamp Renewal: a new Archive Timestamp covers the timestamp of the old one. A series of these forms an Archive Timestamp Chain. It is needed when a timestamp key or algorithm is at risk, and it does not need access to the archived data objects.
  • Hash-Tree Renewal: needed when the hash algorithm of the tree becomes insecure. The data objects and the old chains are hashed together with a new, secure hash algorithm and timestamped, which starts a new chain. Chains together form an Archive Timestamp Sequence.

In a Hash-Tree Renewal, for each object the hash of the data is concatenated with the hash of the DER-encoded earlier chains, and the result is hashed again to give the new leaf. Chains and sequences MUST be ordered ascending by time, and within one chain all reduced hash trees MUST use the same hash algorithm. After renewal, only the most recent Archive Timestamp needs to be watched for expiry and loss of security.
sections.eli5: Re-stamping just the stamp is a quick fix. If the whole stamping method turns weak, you must re-stamp the document and all its old stamps together with a better method.

sections.title: Verifying a Sequence
sections.content:
To prove that a data object existed at a certain time, verification checks the chains and how they link:

  1. The first Archive Timestamp of the first chain contains the hash of the data object.
  2. In each chain, the first hash list of every Archive Timestamp MUST contain the hash of the previous Archive Timestamp's timestamp, each one MUST be valid at the time of the next, and the shared hash algorithm MUST be secure when the following chain's first Archive Timestamp was made.
  3. The first hash list of the first Archive Timestamp of each later chain contains the hash of the data object hash concatenated with the hash of all older chains, and it was generated before the last timestamp of the previous chain became invalid.

To complete the proof, the last Archive Timestamp has to be valid at the time of verification.
sections.eli5: You walk back along the chain of stamps, checking each stamp was still good when the next one was added, until you reach the first one.

sections.title: Encrypted Data and CMS Integration
sections.content:
If clients send only encrypted data to an archive, the record refers to the encrypted bits. ERS freezes the bit structure at archiving time, so the encryption scheme cannot change without losing the integrity proof. A proof about encrypted data cannot always prove the unencrypted data, because a different algorithm or key might be chosen for decryption. So only encryption methods that unambiguously represent the plain data should be used, and the information needed to re-encrypt exactly should be placed in encryptionInfo by the client. The long-term archive never sees those values. The structure holds an object identifier and a value whose meaning must be defined in other specifications.

Appendix A describes how to put a record into CMS signed or enveloped data as an unsigned or unprotected attribute, identified by id-aa-er-internal or id-aa-er-external. Either the whole CMS object is timestamped, or the CMS object and its content are timestamped as a group. When verifying, the record being checked is removed from the object first, while earlier records stay in place.
sections.eli5: If you stamp a locked box, the stamp is about the box. So you must also keep what you need to prove the unlocked thing matches that exact box.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Algorithms and parameters used in Archive Timestamps must be secure at the time they are generated, and verifying components must consider published guidance on algorithm suitability. Some parts of a timestamp may lose their security before this is publicly known, and many timestamp authorities use the same signature algorithms. A compromised private key affects one authority, but a retrospective loss of a signature algorithm can affect many at once.

The RFC therefore recommends at least two redundant Evidence Records that use different hash algorithms and different timestamp authorities with different signature algorithms, ideally managed in a central long-term archive. Renewed Archive Timestamps should be of the same or higher quality than the initial one. For non-repudiation it does not matter whether encryption was broken, but users should keep private keys and random values secret and disclose them only if needed, for example to a judge.
sections.eli5: Do not trust just one stamp-maker. Keep two proofs from different makers, in case one turns out to be unreliable.
